Maya had planned the trip on graph paper. Day one: six miles up the Sawyer Creek trail, cross at the stepping stones, camp at Hatch Lake by four. Day two: swim, then home. Beside the stones she had drawn a small arrow pointing to the meadow on the near bank, and next to it the only word the plan gave that meadow: water. It was where you filled your bottles before the crossing.

It rained the night before we left, hard enough to wake me, and by morning the sky had cleared to a washed blue. Aunt June looked at it from the porch and said nothing, which I took to mean the trip was on.

We reached the creek a little after two. I heard it before I saw it, a low steady roar where the map promised a stream. The stepping stones were somewhere under the brown water. You could find them only by the smooth humps the current made going over them.

"It's knee-deep at most," Maya said. "We can wade."

Aunt June took off her pack. She did not argue. She snapped a dead branch to the length of her forearm, walked ten paces upstream with Maya, handed her the stick, and walked back. "Throw it in there," she called, "and count until it passes me."

Maya threw it. The stick spun once and shot past her mother before she had counted two.

"That's ten paces in under two seconds," Aunt June said. "Now picture that water against the backs of your knees, with a forty-pound pack on." She sat down on a rock and began to unlace her boots, as if the question were settled. Then she said, "You planned it. You decide."

Maya stood at the edge of the water for a long time. Then she threw a second stick, and a third, and counted each one out loud. When the third went by, she walked back up the bank and unbuckled her pack beside her mother's.

We camped in the meadow. It had a flat place for the tent and a view straight down the valley, and at dusk two deer came out of the alders to drink at the creek's edge, thirty feet from where we sat eating. Maya watched them with the plan open on her knees.

In the morning the water had dropped a foot and the stones were showing. We could have crossed. Instead we ate breakfast slowly and walked out the way we had come.

A week later, at their house, I saw the plan pinned above Maya's desk. She had crossed out "water" by the meadow and written, in small careful letters, "camp here."

When the apartment holds the heat
like a closed fist, my father
props the stairwell door with a brick
and we climb the last flight to the roof.

The tar gives a little under our sneakers.
Somebody's tomato plants lean in buckets
against the low wall, and the water tank
stands on its wooden legs like a horse asleep.

Down on the street the city is one block long:
the bodega, the laundromat, the bus
that comes around the corner and is gone.
I have lived my whole life inside that block.

Up here it keeps going.
The avenues run off in lit rows
toward the river, and the bridge
strings its lamps from shore to shore

the way you might hold a necklace up
between your two hands to show its length.
My father names the neighborhoods on the far side
as if they were cousins who never visit.

Across the airshaft, in a hundred windows,
people are doing what we were doing an hour ago:
scrubbing a pot, arguing over the fan,
standing in the cold light of an open refrigerator.

From here they look small and lit and careful,
each one framed, each one busy with an evening
that must seem to them the only evening.
I think we must look like that too.

I would like to call across to all of them
that the pot will come clean,
that the fan will swing back their way,
that someone on a roof can see them.

Somewhere under our feet, our own kitchen
sits dark, its fan still turning.
Tomorrow the block will be one block long again.
Tonight I count the windows and keep losing count.

The summer I was twelve, the woman who lived below us painted the window of Lupo's Bakery, and I watched her do it from the sidewalk for most of a Tuesday. Her name was Inez Calloway, and she had been lettering signs in our part of the city for forty years: the gold numbers on the bank's door, the red script over the shoe store, the menu boards at half the diners on Fulton Avenue.

By Thursday I had asked whether she would teach me, and by the next week I was sitting at her kitchen table with a jar of water, a pot of black paint, and a brush with hairs as long as my little finger.

She began with a single stroke. Load the brush, she said, lay it down, and pull, and let the brush turn the corner instead of your wrist. I filled sheets of newspaper with that one stroke for three afternoons before she let me make a letter.

The lesson I remember best came in August. I had painted the word LOOK across a practice board, and I had measured it with a ruler so that every letter stood exactly the same distance from the next. It looked wrong, and I could see that it looked wrong, but I had done everything right.

Mrs. Calloway stood behind me for a while. Then she took the ruler out of my hand and set it face down on the table.

"The ruler is telling the truth about the space," she said. "Your eye is telling the truth about the word. When they disagree, the person reading the sign will believe the eye."

She showed me what she meant. Because the two O's curve away from each other, the space between them looked wider than it was, almost a hole in the middle of the word. The L, with its open corner, seemed to be drifting away from the rest. She had me paint it again, nudging the O's together and tucking the first one in over the foot of the L, until the gaps looked even, though by the ruler they were all different.

I did not become a sign painter. Most of the shops on Fulton Avenue have plastic signs now, cut by a machine from a computer file. But I still catch myself, in front of a poster or a menu, squinting at the spaces between letters and moving them in my head.

When I left for college, Mrs. Calloway gave me the long brush. It had a strip of tape around the handle with my initials on it. She had put it there, I realized, the first week, before I had painted a single letter.

The summer I was twelve, the woman who lived below us painted the window of Lupo's Bakery, and I watched her do it from the sidewalk for most of a Tuesday. Her name was Inez Calloway, and she had been lettering signs in our part of the city for forty years: the gold numbers on the bank's door, the red script over the shoe store, the menu boards at half the diners on Fulton Avenue.

By Thursday I had asked whether she would teach me, and by the next week I was sitting at her kitchen table with a jar of water, a pot of black paint, and a brush with hairs as long as my little finger.

She began with a single stroke. Load the brush, she said, lay it down, and pull, and let the brush turn the corner instead of your wrist. I filled sheets of newspaper with that one stroke for three afternoons before she let me make a letter.

The lesson I remember best came in August. I had painted the word LOOK across a practice board, and I had measured it with a ruler so that every letter stood exactly the same distance from the next. It looked wrong, and I could see that it looked wrong, but I had done everything right.

Mrs. Calloway stood behind me for a while. Then she took the ruler out of my hand and set it face down on the table.

"The ruler is telling the truth about the space," she said. "Your eye is telling the truth about the word. When they disagree, the person reading the sign will believe the eye."

She showed me what she meant. Because the two O's curve away from each other, the space between them looked wider than it was, almost a hole in the middle of the word. The L, with its open corner, seemed to be drifting away from the rest. She had me paint it again, nudging the O's together and tucking the first one in over the foot of the L, until the gaps looked even, though by the ruler they were all different.

I did not become a sign painter. Most of the shops on Fulton Avenue have plastic signs now, cut by a machine from a computer file. But I still catch myself, in front of a poster or a menu, squinting at the spaces between letters and moving them in my head.

When I left for college, Mrs. Calloway gave me the long brush. It had a strip of tape around the handle with my initials on it. She had put it there, I realized, the first week, before I had painted a single letter.

For thirty-one years the lifeboat at Brenmouth was rowed. Twelve men pulled the Ann Tenby out through the harbor mouth, ten at the oars, with a coxswain at the tiller and a bowman at the front, and in that time they brought something over two hundred people ashore from ships in trouble on the Narrows, a line of sandbanks two miles off the town.

In the autumn of 1912 the regional lifeboat board sent Brenmouth a new boat. The Endeavour was longer and heavier than the Ann Tenby, and amidships, between her oar benches, she carried a forty-horsepower petrol engine in a sealed iron box. With it, the board's letter said, she could reach the Narrows in half the time, against any wind.

The coxswain, a fisherman named Joss Penhale, read the letter aloud in the boathouse and then asked the board's engineer, a young man named Albert Rusk, a single question: what happens when a sea comes over the box? Penhale did not say the engine was useless. He said he wanted to know what it would do in the one place where it mattered.

Rusk said the box was watertight. Penhale asked that the Endeavour carry a full set of oars anyway, and a mast and sail, and that the crew keep up its rowing drills every month as before. The board agreed, though its next letter called the oars "a comfort rather than a necessity." Rusk was asked to come out on the winter drills, and he did, in a borrowed oilskin, seasick for most of January.

The test came on the night of 9 December 1913, when a coal schooner went aground on the outer Narrows in a southwest gale. The Endeavour reached her in thirty-five minutes. The old boat would have needed more than an hour. The lifeboat crew took off all seven men aboard.

On the way back a heavy sea broke over the stern and filled the cockpit. The engine coughed and stopped. For the last mile, in the dark, the crew rowed the Endeavour home, schooner's men and all, on the oars the board had called a comfort.

Rusk's report to the board praised the engine's speed and recommended a better seal for the box. Penhale's entry in the station log is three lines long. It gives the time of launch, the number of men saved, and, on the last line, the words "Engine stopped 11.40. Rowed in." The following year the board's printed rules for motor lifeboats included a new requirement: every such boat was to carry oars.

Some volunteers, shown their own first accounts, insisted that the later version was the true one.

A study run in 2001 added a useful comparison. Along with the shocking news, students were asked to describe an ordinary event from the same few days, such as a party or a study session. Over the following months, both kinds of memory changed at roughly the same rate, gaining new details and losing old ones. What differed was the students' confidence. Their belief in the ordinary memories faded as the details did. Their belief in the dramatic memory stayed high, and the memory went on feeling vivid even as its content drifted.

It appears to do much less for the surrounding details.

None of this means that memory is useless or that vivid memories are always wrong. Most of what people remember about their lives is accurate enough to live by. The research suggests something narrower: that the feeling of being sure is a poor test of whether a memory is correct, and that the brightest memories may be the ones most in need of checking.
